text: Mary Fairchild MacMonnies Low (1858–1946) was an American painter known for her work in landscapes, genre paintings, and portraits. Born in 1858 in New Haven, Connecticut, she studied at the St. Louis School of Fine Arts, where she received a three-year scholarship, and later in Paris at the Académie Julian and under Carolus Duran. She maintained her own studio at 11 Impasse du Maine, which is now part of the Musée Bourdelle. She married Frederick MacMonnies in 1888 and divorced him in 1909, after which she married Will H. Low that same year. In April 1892, Low (then MacMonnies) was approached by Sarah Tyson Hallowell, agent for Bertha Palmer, the key figure behind the Woman's Building at the World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago in 1893, to paint one of two mural tympana for the building's interior; the other was Modern Woman by Mary Cassatt. The subject of Low's mural was Primitive Women, which was considered more successful than Cassatt's at the time, and these were the only murals created by either artist. MacMonnies Low also exhibited her work at the Palace of Fine Arts during the 1893 Exposition. She is represented in the Museum of Rouen, France, where she won a gold medal in 1903 and again in 1911, as well as a gold medal in Dresden in 1902 and in Marseille in 1905, and the Julia Shaw prize from the Society of American Artists in 1902. She became an associate of the National Academy of Design.
